extracted.intended_audience: The People of the State of New York; citizens and readers interested in constitutional design and the structure of the executive
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts (Federalist Nos. 70–73) arguing standards for structuring the national executive: unity, term length, re-eligibility, compensation, appointment power, and the veto. The text sets out normative criteria for a vigorous, independent executive in a republican constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive should be 'ONE' (a single magistrate) rather than a council; multiplication of the Executive is 'rather dangerous than friendly to liberty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments and guidance: A single executive is more easily confined and more safely watched by the people; councils enable combinations of interests, become sources of danger, may clog good intentions, serve as instruments or accomplices of faults, and add expense. Examples/illustration: the Decemvirs of Rome as a dangerous multiplicity; councils can diminish the personal responsibility of the chief magistrate (appropriate in monarchy, improper in a republic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration in Office (term length)
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer duration in office increases the personal firmness of the executive and the stability of administration; a limited but substantial term (discussed as four years) contributes materially to these ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale and effects: Human nature gives a person greater attachment and willingness to risk for what he holds by a durable title; short tenure produces feebleness and irresolution. A term like four years makes independence more likely without unduly endangering liberty; it gives time to establish reputation and to pursue measures that require maturity. It also reduces legislative leverage over the executive that would arise from fear of imminent displacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from the Legislature via Term and Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Term length and constitutional arrangements should secure the Executive's independence from the legislature so that the Executive can 'dare to act his own opinion with vigor and decision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Short duration or direct legislative control (or influence over re-election) makes the Executive susceptible to legislative pressure; the legislature's influence over public opinion can be used to prevent re-election and thereby compromise independence. The partition of powers must make each branch independent of the others, not merely formally separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-eligibility (no constitutional exclusion or disabling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing re-eligibility (not permanently excluding a successful chief magistrate) is important; exclusion (temporary or perpetual) produces several disadvantages and undermines the inducements to good government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments against exclusion: Exclusion diminishes incentives to good behavior (less reward for meritorious service), tempts avarice and peculation if office is transient, deprives the community of experienced leaders in crises, and forces mutability in administration and policy. While exclusion is proposed to increase independence and security, these advantages are speculative and outweighed by certain harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate Provision for Support (fixed compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chief Magistrate must receive a compensation 'which shall neither be increased nor diminished during the period for which he shall have been elected; and he shall not receive within that period any other emolument.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose and mechanism: A fixed salary prevents the legislature from using control over pay to intimidate or seduce the Executive, thereby protecting his independence. Allowing the legislature discretionary control over emoluments would give it power over the Executive's will. The prohibition on other emoluments prevents outside pecuniary influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent Powers: Qualified Negative / Veto Power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive should have a qualified negative upon acts or resolutions of the legislature (a power to return bills with objections, preventing them becoming law unless overridden by two-thirds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions and justification: The qualified negative is both a shield for the Executive against legislative encroachment and a safeguard for the community against improper, hasty, or faction-driven laws. It provides a constitutional arm for the Executive's self-defense and increases the chance of catching legislative errors. Objections and replies: While a single man may not be more virtuous than many, the veto is justified because legislatures are fallible and prone to faction; moreover, the Executive will likely use the veto with caution, making abuse less probable than timidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Control over Administration (appointments and superintendence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who manage executive details (foreign negotiations, finance plans, disbursement of public monies, army and navy arrangements, operations of war) should be assistants or deputies of the chief magistrate, deriving office from his nomination and subject to his superintendence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link to stability: The President's ability to appoint and supervise subordinate officers connects to the stability of administration; frequent change of chief magistrate or lack of control over subordinates leads to mutability of measures and undermines coherent policy. A durable chief magistrate with appointment influence can maintain a consistent system of administration; successors often reverse predecessors when subordinates and appointments are not under the chief's direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of Powers and Mutual Checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Partitioning government into branches must render each independent of the others and furnish them with constitutional arms for self-defense; otherwise separation is nominal and power will be united.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples: The legislature has a natural tendency to absorb other branches; therefore executive and judiciary must have independence (e.g., fixed compensation, veto power) to prevent the legislative authority from becoming predominant. The careful construction of separate powers and checks increases the security of liberty and reduces the risk of concentration of power.
